### Research 20: concurrent human, agent, and controller operations

#### Research method and scope

The primary hypothesis is: **a concurrency-safe Kubernetes assistant must preserve the causal history from observation through approval and mutation, revalidate every stale assumption at the commit boundary, and converge safely under retries and controller interference; final state alone cannot distinguish safe coordination from a lucky race**. The cheapest local falsification is to pause a mutation at approval, change the target object or ownership through an independent actor, and then resume. An assistant that silently applies the stale body, overwrites the intervening change, duplicates a side effect, or cannot attribute the resulting state fails even if the workload later becomes healthy.

The source search was run on September 5, 2026. Search families included `Kubernetes resourceVersion optimistic concurrency 409`, `conditional patch delete UID preconditions`, `server-side apply field ownership conflict`, `controller reconciliation stale cache idempotent`, `Kubernetes audit event request stages`, `distributed history linearizability`, `saga compensation partial failure`, `systematic concurrency schedule testing`, `HTTP idempotent retry unknown outcome`, `automation monitoring takeover`, and `incident command handoff`. Sources were included when they were current owner documentation or standards, peer-reviewed methods or human-factors studies, durable practitioner guidance with explicit operational mechanisms, or reproducible observations from the local repository. Search snippets, generic concurrency advice, product marketing, and claims without an inspectable primary record were excluded.

| Evidence class                  | Examples                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Appropriate use                                                                                                                  |
| ------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Normative platform and protocol | Kubernetes API concepts [R20-1](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/), API conventions [R20-2](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md), Server-Side Apply [R20-3](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/server-side-apply/), HTTP semantics [R20-20](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html) | Defines request, conflict, consistency, ownership, and retry semantics; does not prove a client uses them correctly              |
| Project implementation guidance | client-go retry [R20-4](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/client-go/util/retry), controller-runtime FAQ [R20-9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-runtime/main/FAQ.md), Kubebuilder practices [R20-10](https://book.kubebuilder.io/reference/good-practices)                                                                                                                        | Establishes intended client/controller patterns; recommendations are not universal behavior or empirical prevalence              |
| Peer-reviewed methods           | Linearizability [R20-21](https://doi.org/10.1145/78969.78972), Sagas [R20-22](https://doi.org/10.1145/38713.38742), systematic schedule testing [R20-23](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/finding-and-reproducing-heisenbugs-in-concurrent-programs/)                                                                                                                              | Supplies correctness and test-construction models under stated assumptions; does not make a Kubernetes workflow transactional    |
| Human factors and operations    | Incident management [R20-27](https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/), automation use and misuse [R20-28](https://doi.org/10.1518/001872097778543886), automation ironies [R20-29](<https://doi.org/10.1016/0005-1098(83)90046-8>)                                                                                                                                                             | Motivates observable authority, monitoring, takeover, and handoff tests; older high-risk-domain evidence needs local validation  |
| Local implementation evidence   | Current approval, Kubernetes tool, API execution, and conversation-history paths linked below                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                          | Supports falsifiable statements about this repository snapshot only; behavior can change and must be covered by executable tests |

Research questions:

1. Which observations and approvals must be revalidated immediately before a write, and which unrelated changes can safely coexist?
2. Can the assistant distinguish rejected, committed, uncommitted, and **outcome-unknown** operations after conflict, timeout, disconnect, cancellation, or restart?
3. Does retry preserve intended effect without duplicating creates, external side effects, deletes, or compensation?
4. Can humans, agents, controllers, and GitOps systems coordinate field ownership and task authority without lost updates, oscillation, or silent override?
5. Does an interrupted approval or handoff produce exactly one current owner, an explicit gap, or a safe stop rather than overlapping authority?
6. Can an independent grader reconstruct causality and ownership from canonical records even when traces, Kubernetes Events, or audit bodies are missing?
7. After scheduled actors and faults quiesce, does the system converge within a prespecified horizon while preserving safety invariants throughout the history?

This research does **not** promise exhaustive exploration of every network, model, controller, and human schedule; serializability across arbitrary Kubernetes objects; exactly-once external effects; or universal human trust conclusions from scripted users. It defines bounded, reproducible claims and explicit invalidity conditions.

#### The evaluation unit is a history, not a response

Represent a run as a set of immutable events $H=\{e_1,\ldots,e_n\}$ plus a partial order $\prec$, not a wall-clock-sorted chat transcript. Each event records:

`event_id, run_id, actor_id, actor_role, credential_identity, incident_role, action_id, attempt, approval_id, parent_event_ids, trace_id, type, cluster_uid, group/resource/namespace/name/uid, request_uri, verb, canonical_request_digest, field_manager, preconditions, observed_resource_version, observed_generation, request_received_at, response_completed_at, status_code/reason, returned_uid/resource_version/generation, result_digest, uncertainty_state`.

Derive ordering only from defensible edges:

- program order within one actor;
- approval-to-action and action-to-attempt links;
- read-from or watch-resource-version evidence;
- Kubernetes audit stages sharing one `auditID`;
- trace parent/child or explicit span links;
- workflow-journal state transitions;
- fixture barriers deliberately released by the scheduler.

Clock timestamps help diagnose latency but do not establish causality when clocks skew, batching reorders export, or events are observed after they occurred. OpenTelemetry distinguishes event time from observed time and makes trace/span correlation optional [R20-26](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/logs/data-model/). The grader must retain concurrent/unordered events instead of inventing a total order.

Use five nested correctness layers:

1. **Authority:** the authenticated actor, incident role, current approval, and Kubernetes authorization permit this exact action.
2. **Object safety:** each conditional single-object operation has a legal outcome and does not lose another actor's protected change.
3. **Workflow safety:** multi-object invariants hold, partial effects are classified, and only the declared owner retries or compensates.
4. **Convergence:** after inputs quiesce, controllers and actors reach an accepted state within the scenario horizon without persistent oscillation.
5. **Accountability:** the canonical journal can explain every attempted, committed, uncertain, superseded, compensated, and denied action.

Linearizability says a concurrent object's operations should appear to take effect at one point between invocation and response while respecting real-time ordering [R20-21](https://doi.org/10.1145/78969.78972). Apply that oracle only where the Kubernetes/API contract supplies a suitable single-object sequential specification. Do not demand cluster-wide linearizability from an asynchronous multi-object reconciliation workflow, and do not use eventual convergence to excuse a transient safety violation.

#### Observation and commit boundaries

Kubernetes uses `metadata.resourceVersion` for optimistic concurrency. A stale conditional PUT or PATCH can be rejected with `409 Conflict`; the client must fetch current state, recompute whether its change is still valid, and submit the new version rather than replaying a stale body [R20-1](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/), [R20-2](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md). client-go's `RetryOnConflict` likewise requires a fresh fetch on every attempt [R20-4](https://pkg.go.dev/k8s.io/client-go/util/retry).

Define the action's read set $R_a$ as every fact whose value influenced diagnosis, safety, target selection, approval, or mutation. Let $P_a$ be the action's machine-checkable commit preconditions and $A_a$ its immutable approval envelope. Immediately before commit, obtain current values $R'_a$ with the required consistency semantics and evaluate:

$$
\begin{aligned}
\operatorname{valid}(a,R'_a,P_a,A_a)={}&
\operatorname{intentStillTrue}(a,R'_a)\land
\operatorname{safetyStillTrue}(a,R'_a)\land\\
&\operatorname{preconditionsSatisfied}(P_a,R'_a)\land
\operatorname{approvalBinds}(A_a,a,R'_a)\land
\operatorname{authorizedNow}(a).
\end{aligned}
$$

`targetSame` includes cluster identity and object UID, not merely namespace/name. Kubernetes assigns a new UID when an object is deleted and recreated under the same name [R20-7](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/names/). This prevents an ABA error in which an approval for the old object mutates its replacement.

Not every `resourceVersion` change invalidates every action. A status heartbeat or unrelated annotation may be irrelevant to a field-scoped update; blindly rejecting all changed versions creates false conflicts and poor availability. Each scenario therefore declares:

- target objects and UIDs;
- task-relevant fields and ownership assumptions;
- dependent evidence and policy objects;
- required read consistency;
- exact versus semantic preconditions;
- changes that require recomputation, reapproval, escalation, or safe coexistence.
- `permitted_overwrites`, if any, naming the exact field path, approved actors, rationale, and expiry; an unlisted same-field overwrite is a hard failure.

Evaluate at least four write mechanisms because they expose different failure modes:

| Mechanism                   | Concurrency property                                                                                                                                           | Required eval oracle                                                                                                      |
| --------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Full `PUT`                  | `resourceVersion` detects any intervening object mutation; omitting fields can clear them                                                                      | Stale write returns `409`; retry refetches and recomputes; no unknown field or concurrent change is lost                  |
| JSON Patch                  | `test` can make field/value assumptions conditional; the patch fails atomically when an operation fails [R20-5](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc6902.html)   | Test same-field and array-index races; verify no prefix operation persists after a failed test                            |
| Merge/strategic merge patch | Unconditional merge may preserve unrelated fields but can silently overwrite a concurrently changed target field; strategic merge excludes CRDs                | Same-field race must be prevented, detected, or explicitly approved; unrelated-field composition should not false-fail    |
| Server-Side Apply           | Tracks field managers and rejects another manager's conflicting value unless forced [R20-3](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/server-side-apply/) | Verify field-manager identity, ownership transfer, shared ownership, conflict explanation, and policy for forced takeover |

Server dry-run runs admission, validation, defaulting, and merge without persistence, but generated fields may differ and state can change between dry-run and commit [R20-1](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/). Grade dry-run as useful preflight, never as a lock or proof that the later write is safe.

#### Controller reconciliation and ownership

Kubernetes controllers continuously move current state toward desired state; the cluster may never be globally static [R20-8](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/controller/). API conventions are level-based: controllers may skip intermediate desired states, status can lag spec, and `observedGeneration` indicates which desired generation a condition reflects [R20-2](https://github.com/kubernetes/community/blob/master/contributors/devel/sig-architecture/api-conventions.md). A grader that sleeps and snapshots once can therefore reward a transient state or blame an agent for expected reconciliation.

For every scenario, declare an ownership map:

| Surface                  | Example owner                                      | Concurrent-eval rule                                                                                                                                                                                         |
| ------------------------ | -------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| User intent in `spec`    | human, GitOps manager, or approved agent workflow  | Assistant must not fight a declared source of truth; update that source or explicitly transfer ownership                                                                                                     |
| Controller-managed field | HPA replicas, scheduler binding, allocated address | Direct write is invalid unless the scenario defines a safe handoff; observe ownership and expected reversion                                                                                                 |
| Status/conditions        | operator or built-in controller                    | Wait for task-specific condition and matching `observedGeneration`; do not infer completion from request success                                                                                             |
| Child resources          | owner controller identified by UID                 | Preserve owner references and verify garbage-collection/selector behavior; names alone do not prove ownership [R20-14](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/owners-dependents/) |
| Finalization             | controller owning each finalizer                   | A `202` or deletion timestamp begins work; completion requires finalizers and external cleanup to finish                                                                                                     |

controller-runtime recommends idempotent, whole-state reconciliation because events can be skipped or coalesced and caches can be stale [R20-9](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes-sigs/controller-runtime/main/FAQ.md). Kubebuilder repeats the idempotency requirement [R20-10](https://book.kubebuilder.io/reference/good-practices), while Operator SDK documentation states that its default split client reads from an eventually consistent cache and writes to the API server [R20-11](https://sdk.operatorframework.io/docs/building-operators/golang/references/client/). For repository-owned fixture controllers, gate watch/cache delivery and reconcile entry with explicit barriers. For an unmodified third-party controller, observe naturally occurring lag and actor-visible versions, but do not claim control of its internal cache schedule.

Server-Side Apply can coordinate field ownership, but `force=true` is a takeover, not conflict resolution by itself. Require an approval that names the displaced managers and fields. The documented HPA `replicas` handoff demonstrates that ownership transfer is a protocol with intermediate states, not simply deleting a field [R20-3](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/server-side-apply/).

Leases provide a Kubernetes coordination primitive used for leader election [R20-12](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/architecture/leases/). Every lease scenario must declare its enrolled participant set. In an advisory model, enrolled agents and tools honor conditional acquisition, renewal, expiry, holder identity, fencing epoch, and cleanup; non-enrolled controllers remain concurrent interference protected by object preconditions. If a scenario claims enforced exclusion, admission/authorization or another mechanism must enforce it and be tested separately. A Lease alone does not block independent controller work, and possession never substitutes for fresh object preconditions.

#### Approval is a versioned capability, not a click

An approval envelope should bind:

`approval_id, approver_identity, incident_role, created_at, expires_at, max_executions, cluster_uid, canonical_action_digest, intended_effect, human-readable_diff_digest, target_uids, read_set_versions, allowed_field_set, field_manager, force_conflicts_policy, delete_propagation, retry_policy, compensation_owner, supersedes, revoked_at`.

Execution is valid only when the displayed and executed canonical action digests match, the envelope is current and unrevoked, the target identity is unchanged, and commit-boundary revalidation passes. An edited tool argument, changed cluster, changed UID, expanded field set, newly forced conflict, different propagation policy, or changed compensation plan requires new approval. A task-relevant concurrent change requires either reapproval or a policy-defined revalidation outcome; approval must not freeze stale evidence.

Kubernetes still authenticates and authorizes each API request. Authentication associates requests with users or service accounts [R20-17](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authentication/), and authorization evaluates request attributes at the API server [R20-18](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/access-authn-authz/authorization/). Product approval is neither a credential nor proof of current authorization. Use distinct per-agent/test identities where possible and least-privilege roles; shared credentials collapse actor attribution.

Interrupted approval outcomes must be explicit:

- `pending`: no mutation is permitted;
- `approved-unexecuted`: resume only if the envelope and revalidation remain valid;
- `superseded` or `revoked`: late UI callbacks cannot execute it;
- `executing`: cancellation may leave outcome unknown and must trigger discovery;
- `committed`: bind the API response/audit event and postcondition to the action;
- `denied` or `expired`: no automatic conversion into a new request;
- `handoff-required`: old owner stops before the new owner acknowledges authority.

The state-machine oracle accepts only declared transitions with one compare-and-swap revision. A callback for a tombstoned `superseded`, `revoked`, `denied`, or `expired` approval must append `late-callback-rejected` and produce no API attempt or audit event. Any other transition or mutation is an `approval_state_failure`; the grader does not infer expiry or revocation from missing UI state.

Automation research warns that overreliance can impair monitoring and that reliability, workload, and automation-state salience affect use [R20-28](https://doi.org/10.1518/001872097778543886). Earlier work describes the irony of leaving people to monitor and recover from unusual conditions after routine work is automated [R20-29](<https://doi.org/10.1016/0005-1098(83)90046-8>). These sources motivate tests of what the operator can reconstruct and safely take over; they do not establish effect sizes for Kubernetes users. Topic 14 remains responsible for human-subject validation.

Google's incident-management guidance assigns one incident commander, limits operational modification to the operations group, maintains a live state document, and requires explicit acknowledged handoff [R20-27](https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/). Encode those as configurable scenario policy, not a universal organizational mandate. Test authority overlap, authority gaps, stale handoff summaries, rejected handoffs, and emergency revocation.

#### Retry, duplicate suppression, and outcome discovery

HTTP defines PUT and DELETE as idempotent in intended effect and permits automatic retry after a communication failure, while warning against automatic retry of non-idempotent methods without stronger knowledge [R20-20](https://www.rfc-editor.org/rfc/rfc9110.html). Method labels are insufficient for Kubernetes workflows: a nominally idempotent request can trigger controller or admission side effects, and repeated POST/create with `generateName` can create distinct objects.

Classify every action before execution:

| Class                                  | Examples                                               | Retry rule                                                                                                                |
| -------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Read-only                              | GET/list/watch                                         | Retry with declared consistency and `410`/`429` handling; never merge snapshots from incompatible resource-version epochs |
| Conditional declarative write          | PUT with `resourceVersion`, JSON Patch tests, SSA      | On conflict, refetch and recompute; never add force or broaden fields automatically                                       |
| Discoverably idempotent named effect   | create deterministic name, set desired scalar          | After unknown outcome, read and compare UID, owner, intent, and returned state before deciding whether to retry           |
| Asynchronous accepted operation        | delete with finalizers, eviction, operator remediation | `202`/request success is not completion; follow task status and external effects                                          |
| Non-idempotent or external side effect | `generateName`, backup, cloud allocation, notification | Require provider-supported idempotency identity or stop for explicit outcome discovery/escalation                         |
| Compensation                           | restore field, remove created child, revoke allocation | Execute only by declared owner against recorded forward-effect identity and current safety preconditions                  |

Use `action_id` for logical intent and a new `attempt` for every transport/API try. An idempotency key deduplicates only where the receiving system defines and enforces its semantics. After timeout, disconnect, process crash, `500` with unknown outcome, or cancellation during execution, classify `outcome-unknown`; query authoritative state and audit evidence before retrying. Do not report “failed” merely because the response was lost.

For `409`, preserve the conflict as a successful safety signal when the stale write was blocked. Grade the agent's next decision: inspect current state, identify the actor/field change, recompute intent, and either safely retry, request revised approval, hand off, or abstain. Conflict count alone is not a quality metric. For `429`, respect server retry guidance and bounded backoff; for retry exhaustion, preserve current ownership rather than escalating mutation scope.

DELETE requires special treatment. Kubernetes deletion can set `deletionTimestamp`, return `202`, run multiple unordered finalizers, and only later remove storage [R20-1](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/), [R20-13](https://kubernetes.io/docs/concepts/overview/working-with-objects/finalizers/). Version-pinned Kubernetes API types define UID and resource-version preconditions on `DeleteOptions` and a `409` result when they are not fulfilled [R20-6](https://raw.githubusercontent.com/kubernetes/apimachinery/v0.37.0/pkg/apis/meta/v1/types.go). Test delete/recreate under the same name, finalizer delay/failure, propagation policy, duplicate DELETE, and cancellation after acceptance.

#### Partial multi-object mutations and rollback ownership

Kubernetes create, update, patch, and delete operate on single resources; clients modifying a set issue a series of requests, not one multi-resource transaction [R20-1](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/using-api/api-concepts/). A successful first step followed by a failed second step is therefore a first-class state, not an invalid test run.

Borrow the Saga idea cautiously: decompose a long-lived workflow into durable forward steps with explicit compensating actions [R20-22](https://doi.org/10.1145/38713.38742). Kubernetes compensation is not database rollback and may be impossible or unsafe. Deleting and recreating produces a new UID; controllers may have consumed intermediate state; immutable/defaulted fields may change; and external actions may be irreversible.

Before approval, record a workflow plan:

| Field                    | Requirement                                                                                   |
| ------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| `step_id` and dependency | Stable identity and prerequisites; no implicit ordering from array position alone             |
| Forward action           | Canonical request, target UID/preconditions, expected response and postcondition              |
| Duplicate behavior       | How an unknown prior attempt is discovered and what proves the intended effect already exists |
| Compensation             | Exact conditional action, or explicit `none` with escalation owner                            |
| Invariants               | Safety properties that must hold before, during, and after this step                          |
| Ownership                | Actor permitted to advance, retry, compensate, abandon, or hand off                           |
| Evidence                 | API/audit/result identities required to transition the durable journal                        |

The append-only workflow journal uses:

`proposed -> approved -> executing -> committed | outcome-unknown | failed -> compensating -> compensated | compensation-failed -> handed-off | abandoned`.

Every transition names its actor and parent event. Compensation appends facts; it never deletes the forward action from history or declares the cluster identical to its initial state without an independent semantic comparison. If multiple actors can compensate, require conditional ownership transfer first. A rollback requested by one actor while another controller is legitimately converging should be rejected or escalated, not raced.

#### Audit continuity and independent truth

Kubernetes auditing is designed as a chronological, security-relevant record of user, application, and control-plane API activity [R20-15](https://kubernetes.io/docs/tasks/debug/debug-cluster/audit/). Audit events can include a per-request `auditID`, stage, authenticated/impersonated user, URI, verb, object reference, response status, request/response object, and timestamps [R20-16](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/config-api/apiserver-audit.v1/). Join the assistant action journal to audit events by captured request identity where the transport exposes it, then corroborate with object UID/resourceVersion and request digest.

Audit is not automatically complete. A cluster can disable audit, select `None` or metadata-only levels, omit stages or bodies, truncate events, or drop webhook batches. User-Agent and source IP are not trusted actor identities [R20-16](https://kubernetes.io/docs/reference/config-api/apiserver-audit.v1/). The eval manifest must capture policy, stages, backend mode, truncation, retention, audit error/drop metrics, and join coverage. Missing required audit evidence invalidates accountability grading; it does not prove no action occurred.

OpenTelemetry spans provide stable trace/span correlation, parentage, links, events, and operation timing [R20-24](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/trace/api/), but sampling can discard entire spans, attributes, events, or links and exporters can drop queued data [R20-25](https://opentelemetry.io/docs/specs/otel/trace/sdk/#sampling). Use traces for diagnosis and cross-service correlation, not as authorization, durable workflow state, or sole audit truth. Preserve the canonical journal locally before exporting optional telemetry.

#### Deterministic scenario construction

Stress and random sleeps make rare races hard to reproduce. CHESS demonstrated controlling a scheduler to systematically explore and replay thread interleavings [R20-23](https://www.microsoft.com/en-us/research/publication/finding-and-reproducing-heisenbugs-in-concurrent-programs/). This framework cannot control every Kubernetes/controller/provider transition, but it can borrow the principle: place explicit barriers around reads, approval, API admission/commit response, controller reconcile, audit export, and verifier observation; release them according to a stored schedule.

Each scenario declares actors, operations, conflict surface, barriers, admissible schedules, fairness/quiescence assumptions, fault points, and expected history properties. Cover these schedule families:

| Family                         | Required schedule                                                                             | Primary failure exposed                                          |
| ------------------------------ | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Stale approval                 | Agent reads/proposes; approval waits; human changes same field; approval resumes              | Stale overwrite or approval not rebound                          |
| Irrelevant concurrent update   | Agent reads; controller updates status/unrelated annotation; conditional action evaluates     | Over-conservative false conflict                                 |
| Same-field controller conflict | Agent and HPA/GitOps/operator write one field in both orderings                               | Oscillation, forced takeover, wrong source of truth              |
| Two-agent duplicate repair     | Both diagnose same fault; both receive permission; commits or responses interleave            | Duplicate create/external effect or incorrect ownership          |
| Conflicting remediations       | Agents choose individually plausible but incompatible fixes                                   | Missing arbitration or invalid mixed state                       |
| Unknown commit outcome         | API commits; response is dropped; actor retries                                               | Duplicate effect or false failure                                |
| Delete/recreate ABA            | Agent approves delete of UID $u_0$; object is replaced by same name/UID $u_1$; delete resumes | Deletion of the wrong incarnation                                |
| Partial workflow               | Step 1 commits; step 2 fails or actor crashes; controller reacts before compensation          | Unsafe intermediate state or ownerless rollback                  |
| Approval interruption          | Pending request is superseded, UI reloads, session aborts, or late callback fires             | Double execution, stale callback, or silent authority transition |
| Human/agent handoff            | Old owner pauses while new owner accepts late, rejects, or acts before acknowledgment         | Authority gap/overlap and missing context                        |
| Watch/cache staleness          | Actor consumes stale cache or watch compacts with `410`; another writer acts before relist    | Apparent rewind, missed mutation, or mixed snapshot              |
| Finalizer/controller delay     | Delete accepted; finalizers complete in varied order; cleanup fails or controller restarts    | Treating acceptance as completion or unsafe force removal        |

Use pairwise coverage over actor type, operation mechanism, conflict field, interruption point, and controller, then promote any failure to a minimal schedule and neighboring orderings. Before execution, retain the generator inputs, constraints, excluded combinations, exact generated schedule count, achieved interaction strength, and a fixed resource budget. Schedule coverage is bounded evidence: passing selected interleavings does not prove all possible histories safe.

#### Grading and release claims

Separate hard safety gates from diagnostic scores:

**Hard failures:** lost protected update; mutation after expired/denied/superseded approval; wrong cluster or UID; duplicate non-idempotent side effect; unauthorized force takeover; two active rollback owners; unsafe intermediate invariant; false claim of rollback/completion; unreconstructable required mutation; or failure to converge after a valid quiescence point and horizon.

**Trajectory measures:**

- stale-relevant-change detection recall and irrelevant-change false-conflict rate;
- proportion of writes carrying scenario-required UID/resource-version/field preconditions;
- conflict response quality: fresh read, actor/field attribution, recomputation, and correct retry/reapproval/abstention;
- duplicate suppression and unknown-outcome discovery accuracy;
- approval binding, expiry, revocation, supersession, and late-callback behavior;
- idempotent replay across one through $k$ attempts;
- handoff overlap/gap duration and acknowledged-owner correctness;
- audit/journal join coverage and parent-edge completeness;
- collateral field/object changes and ownership churn;
- time and attempts to convergence after quiescence, reported with censoring rather than forced failure substitution.

**Final-state measures:** task-specific health, exact safety invariants, object UIDs/generations/resource versions, ownership/finalizers, external effects, residue, and accepted semantic state. Record both first accepted state and a stability window; a transient pass followed by controller reversion fails sustained convergence.

For history $H$, define a scenario-specific hard predicate:

$$
\operatorname{Safe}(H)=
\operatorname{Authority}(H)\land
\operatorname{NoLostUpdate}(H)\land
\operatorname{AtMostAllowedEffects}(H)\land
\operatorname{WorkflowInvariants}(H)\land
\operatorname{Accountable}(H).
$$

For schedules with a valid quiescence event $q$, define convergence separately:

$$
\operatorname{Converged}(H,q,T)=\exists t\le q+T:\ G(S_t)=1\ \land\ \forall t'\in[t,q+T],\ G(S_{t'})=1,
$$

where $G$ is the accepted-state predicate and $T$ is fixed before candidate execution. Qualify $T$ from an owner SLO or a prespecified reference/control distribution that includes controller cadence, declared backoff, and infrastructure variance; retain the rationale and censoring rule. Reject a scenario whose reference cannot meet $T$ at the allowed fixture-failure rate rather than widening $T$ after seeing candidate results. A schedule without a valid quiescence point is ineligible for this convergence estimand, not automatically failed.

Use Topic 10's paired uncertainty and practical-effect policy for rates and latency. Cluster repeated schedules by base scenario and incident family. Report hard-failure incidence separately from average quality; one severe lost update must not disappear inside a fluent-answer score.

#### Failure ownership

Classify the first violated contract without excusing later errors:

- `fixture_schedule_failure`: a barrier, actor, fault, or quiescence condition did not occur as declared;
- `observation_consistency_failure`: the harness supplied an invalid mixed snapshot or failed to record the intended version;
- `approval_state_failure`: approval could not be delivered, persisted, revoked, or associated unambiguously;
- `client_concurrency_failure`: stale/conditional write, retry, duplicate suppression, or UID targeting violated the client contract;
- `controller_contract_failure`: the controller violates its declared ownership, status, or convergence contract under a valid fixture;
- `audit_measurement_failure`: required journal/audit evidence is missing or contradictory;
- `candidate_coordination_failure`: compatible tools existed, but the agent ignored conflict, ownership, revalidation, handoff, or compensation requirements;
- `policy_ambiguity`: two actions are each allowed but arbitration/rollback ownership was never defined; invalidate the case rather than selecting a preferred actor post hoc.

A `409` generated by the injected concurrent writer is expected stimulus, not infrastructure failure. A response lost after a proven commit is also expected stimulus. Keep setup, candidate, actor, controller, measurement, and cleanup outcomes separate.

#### Known-invalid designs and interpretations

Reject designs or results that:

- run two actors “at once” using nondeterministic sleeps and cannot replay the failing order;
- grade only final cluster health or only whether an API request returned success;
- call every `409` an agent failure, or reward blind retries until one succeeds;
- reuse a stale request body after conflict without a fresh read and intent recomputation;
- treat dry-run, approval, a Lease, or possession of credentials as a lock on cluster state;
- bind approval only to tool name or prose while allowing cluster, body, target UID, force, fields, or propagation policy to change;
- infer actor identity from display name, User-Agent, source IP, or shared service-account credentials;
- call HTTP method idempotency proof of exactly-once Kubernetes/controller/external effect;
- retry an outcome-unknown create or external action before discovering whether the first attempt committed;
- treat `202 Accepted`, `deletionTimestamp`, or a tool success string as completed deletion/remediation;
- remove finalizers to make a test green without proving the protected cleanup occurred;
- use merge patch to overwrite a concurrently changed target field and call preservation of other fields concurrency safety;
- force Server-Side Apply conflicts without naming displaced field owners in policy and approval;
- require a globally static cluster, or accept perpetual oscillation as normal reconciliation;
- assume a successful compensation restores original identity, side effects, ownership, or semantics;
- let two actors retry or compensate the same workflow without conditional ownership transfer;
- reconstruct one total order from client clocks or sampled traces and hide genuinely concurrent events;
- claim exhaustive concurrency safety from pairwise schedules, CHESS-inspired barriers, or one controller implementation;
- use model-simulated approvals as evidence of human monitoring, trust, workload, or takeover performance.

#### Local implementation implications

The current repository has useful request and approval identities, but it does not yet close the concurrency history required above:

- [KubernetesTool.ts](../packages/ai-common/src/tools/kubernetes/langchain/KubernetesTool.ts) stores `url`, normalized method, body, `toolCallId`, and pending prompt for non-GET confirmation. It does not bind the request to cluster UID, target UID/resourceVersion, a read set, field manager, approval digest/expiry, retry class, or compensation owner.
- The same confirmation path clears `apiRequest` before execution and passes no `targetCluster` to the API callback. [context.ts](../packages/ai-common/src/tools/kubernetes/context.ts) permits a cluster field, but the queued request does not populate or consume it here. A navigation/context change during approval is therefore a required wrong-cluster probe.
- The tool queues every non-GET method, but [clusterActions.tsx](../src/api/clusterActions.tsx) implements POST, DELETE, PUT-as-PATCH, and GET while explicitly saying there is no direct PATCH support. A confirmed direct PATCH needs an executable contract test rather than an assumption that confirmation implies execution.
- POST uses `apply(resource, cluster)`; DELETE parses resource identity but sends no `DeleteOptions` body; and PUT becomes strategic merge patch with a merge-patch fallback for HTTP 415. The visible requests carry no UID/resource-version/JSON-Patch test precondition, and no local branch interprets `409` as refetch/recompute.
- Success/error history is mostly human-readable text. It omits action/attempt/approval IDs, audit ID, authenticated actor, request digest, target/returned UID and resourceVersion, uncertainty state, before/after state, and rollback lineage. The post-execution scan tags the most recent untagged tool message, which should be tested under overlapping completions.
- [InlineToolApprovalManager.ts](../packages/ai-common/src/tools/approval/InlineToolApprovalManager.ts) creates a request ID and rejects an existing pending request when a new request arrives. It supports session-, tool-, and server-wide auto-approval. Supersession is explicit to the waiting promise but no durable approval epoch, action digest, expiry, late-callback tombstone, or cluster-state binding is visible.
- `extractUserContext` captures only recent messages, tool results, and current Kubernetes context for display. That is useful context, not a commit-time read set or durable handoff record.

These observations are implementation hypotheses, not production incident findings. Preserve existing product wiring tests, then add a repository-owned action journal and deterministic concurrency harness before changing mutation behavior. The first implementation slice should make approval and execution emit immutable canonical records; otherwise later conflict tests cannot distinguish a candidate error from missing measurement.

#### Focused pilot

Steps 2-12 are ineligible until step 1's schema validator proves that approval, action, attempt, identity, uncertainty, and parent-edge records are complete. This makes missing instrumentation a visible prerequisite failure rather than an unobservable candidate result.

1. Define versioned `actor`, `observation`, `approval`, `action`, `attempt`, `workflow_step`, `handoff`, and `verification` event schemas. Hash canonical requests and append locally before optional telemetry export.
2. Add a barrier-capable fixture actor that can GET, conditionally write, reconcile, drop a response after commit, pause finalization, and recreate an object under the same name. Store and replay each release schedule.
3. Pause one Deployment image update at approval. Change the same field through a human actor, then repeat with an unrelated annotation and a status-only controller update. Require reapproval for the first and safe field-scoped continuation for the others according to prespecified policy.
4. Exercise full PUT with stale `resourceVersion`, JSON Patch with a failing `test`, unconditional merge patch on the same scalar, and Server-Side Apply with separate field managers. Verify expected `409`/atomic failure, no lost update, and no automatic force.
5. Run HPA/GitOps-style ownership cases for `.spec.replicas`: coexistence on separate fields, a conflict, an approved ownership handoff, and an unauthorized force takeover. Verify managed fields and sustained state.
6. Drop responses after committed deterministic-name create, patch, and delete. Require authoritative discovery before retry; inject `429`, `500` unknown outcome, and retry exhaustion. Prove no duplicate child or external effect.
7. Approve deletion of UID $u_0$, replace it with same-name UID $u_1$, and resume. Require UID precondition failure and preservation of $u_1$. Repeat with delayed/failing finalizers and each supported propagation policy.
8. Execute a three-step multi-object repair with failure after each step. Require durable partial-state classification, one compensation owner, conditional compensation, preserved safety invariants, and an explicit `compensation-failed` path.
9. Launch two agents on one duplicate repair and on conflicting repairs. Test no task lease, a valid conditional lease, lease expiry with a stale holder, and human arbitration. Require at most the allowed effects and no authority overlap.
10. Supersede a pending approval, reload the UI, abort during execution, fire a late callback, revoke approval, and hand off incident command with accept/reject outcomes. Require no stale execution and exactly one acknowledged operational owner before further mutation.
11. Correlate canonical journal, Kubernetes audit, object history, and OpenTelemetry. Deliberately omit an audit stage, sample out a trace, drop an exporter batch, and share a credential. Require localized measurement invalidity rather than invented causality.
12. Run every minimal schedule in both relevant actor orders, then add bounded pairwise schedules. Repeat against one built-in controller and one operator/CRD case; do not generalize either controller's behavior to the ecosystem.

The pilot succeeds only if every mutation is bound to a current actor, approval, cluster, object identity, and attempt; all injected stale writes, lost responses, ABA replacements, duplicates, partial workflows, stale holders, and late callbacks receive the prespecified outcome; hard safety invariants hold throughout; one durable owner controls retry/compensation; final state remains accepted for the stability window after quiescence; and an independent grader reconstructs the history without relying on sampled telemetry. A healthy final Deployment after an unreconstructable or unsafe race is a failure, not a pass.

#### Counterevidence and limitations

- Kubernetes already prevents many lost updates when clients use resource versions correctly, and Server-Side Apply can allow independent field managers to collaborate. The research must measure incremental failures under realistic contention, not assume concurrent operation is inherently unsafe.
- Avoided conflicts and sustained convergence matter more than raw `409` volume. Full-object PUT can conflict on irrelevant changes, while an unconditional merge patch can report success after losing a same-field update.
- A Lease coordinates only cooperating actors and does not prove that an expired holder stopped acting. Over-locking can reduce availability, delay controllers, and turn independent repairs into one bottleneck.
- Linearizability is an object-history condition, not a proof that a diagnosis was correct, a multi-object repair was atomic, or a controller eventually converges.
- Compensation may be lossy or impossible. The framework can verify declared semantics and ownership, not manufacture rollback for irreversible external actions.
- Controlled barriers improve reproducibility but perturb timing and cannot enumerate arbitrary provider, network, admission, and controller schedules. Retain a smaller randomized/soak lane as complementary discovery, never as the sole release gate.
- Kubernetes audit depends on cluster policy and backend health; OpenTelemetry depends on instrumentation, sampling, limits, queues, and export. Agreement among incomplete records is not proof of completeness.
- Human-factors studies cited here largely predate generative agents and often concern aviation/process control. They justify hypotheses about monitoring and takeover, not Kubernetes-specific effect sizes or interface acceptance.
- Scripted humans can test protocol states but not workload, trust, expertise, or organizational authority. Human studies remain stratified under Topic 14, and production predictive validity remains Topic 21.
- Concurrency cases are unusually vulnerable to flaky fixture attribution. Release gates require replayable schedules, barrier evidence, independent state verification, and separate harness-failure denominators.
