### Research 21: offline-to-deployment predictive validity

#### Research method and scope

Keep two falsifiable hypotheses separate:

- **Predictive-validity hypothesis:** for one named outcome and horizon, a versioned offline metric and frozen prediction rule meet prespecified discrimination, calibration (when probabilistic), coverage, and practical-utility margins in a privacy-reviewed prospective target cohort and remain within revalidation bounds over declared time/cohort shifts.
- **Impact-validity hypothesis:** assignment to one frozen metric-informed candidate policy improves a prespecified operator or system outcome by at least its practical margin relative to the declared baseline policy, without violating hard safety or privacy guardrails.

The cheapest predictive falsification is to freeze one offline score and prediction rule before a bounded shadow cohort, then test it against independent adjudication. The cheapest impact falsification is a later bounded randomized or identified staged comparison in which candidate exposure can change behavior. Failure to meet a predictive margin rejects that predictive claim; null or harmful eligible impact rejects the deployment-benefit claim, while an inconclusive impact study leaves it unvalidated. Retrospective correlation or benchmark improvement alone establishes neither claim.

The source search was run on September 5, 2026. Search families included `offline online metric correlation deployment outcome`, `external prediction validation calibration discrimination`, `prediction model impact study net benefit`, `shadow mode silent deployment counterfactual`, `target trial observational intervention`, `stepped wedge cluster rollout`, `interrupted time series intervention`, `logged policy off-policy evaluation propensity`, `selective labels human decisions`, `dataset shift detection`, `transportability data fusion`, `incident duration censoring competing risk`, `AI post-deployment monitoring`, and `privacy-preserving production feedback`. Sources were included when they were standards or regulator/government frameworks, peer-reviewed statistical or empirical research, durable first-party operational guidance, or reproducible local-code observations. Search snippets, vendor claims without methods, benchmark leaderboards, retrospective anecdotes without denominators, and unrelated papers returned by title/DOI search were excluded. DOI titles and publication identities were checked against Crossref or publisher records before use.

| Evidence class                 | Examples                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                    | Appropriate use                                                                                                                                       |
| ------------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Risk and governance frameworks | NIST AI RMF [R21-1](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), NIST Generative AI Profile [R21-2](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1), NIST Privacy Framework [R21-3](https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework)                                                                                                                                                                                               | Defines lifecycle, monitoring, governance, and privacy questions; voluntary guidance does not validate a metric or product                            |
| Prediction-validation methods  | TRIPOD [R21-4](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.g7594), calibration guidance [R21-5](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-019-1466-7), decision curves [R21-6](https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X06295361)                                                                                                                                                                                                               | Supports transparent prospective prediction and utility analysis by analogy; clinical examples are not evidence about Kubernetes                      |
| Causal and quasi-experimental  | Target-trial emulation [R21-8](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwv254), propensity scores [R21-9](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/70.1.41), interrupted time series [R21-10](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw098), stepped wedge [R21-11](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.h391)                                                                                                                                       | Defines identifiable impact estimands and assumptions when randomized or staged rollout is feasible; no design repairs missing outcomes or bad labels |
| Production ML and empirical    | Google ML guidance [R21-13](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml), hidden technical debt [R21-14](https://research.google/pubs/hidden-technical-debt-in-machine-learning-systems/), offline/online recommender studies [R21-17](https://doi.org/10.1145/2645710.2645745), [R21-18](https://doi.org/10.1145/2792838.2800184), [R21-19](https://doi.org/10.1145/3298689.3347032) | Supplies concrete mismatch mechanisms and domain-specific empirical examples; findings do not transfer automatically to incident-response agents      |
| Reporting and documentation    | STROBE [R21-7](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.39335.541782.AD), Model Cards [R21-25](https://doi.org/10.1145/3287560.3287596), Datasheets [R21-26](https://doi.org/10.1145/3458723)                                                                                                                                                                                                                            | Makes populations, missingness, intended use, subgroup results, and limitations auditable; reporting quality is not outcome validity                  |
| Local implementation evidence  | Current E2E, conversation, and proactive-diagnosis files linked below                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                                       | Establishes missing linkage fields in this repository snapshot only; it is not a production telemetry or incident study                               |

Research questions:

1. Do frozen offline metrics predict later independently adjudicated outcomes for the same unit of deployment decision: release, session, incident, recommendation, or action?
2. Are probabilities and risk bands calibrated overall, by prespecified operator/cluster/incident strata, and across time, or do they only rank cases?
3. Does a shadow candidate add predictive information beyond the production baseline, incident severity, operator expertise, environment, and workflow?
4. When candidate output becomes visible or actionable, does assignment to it improve outcomes relative to the declared policy, not merely correlate with easier cases?
5. Which eligible populations are absent from telemetry, linkage, labels, support channels, or experiments, and under what assumptions can results transport to them?
6. Do offline, shadow, and live failure taxonomies cover production failures, near misses, abstentions, and invalid runs without labels being changed after results are known?
7. Which metrics should be recalibrated, revised into new versions, suspended, or retired when offline gains fail to produce deployment benefit?

This section treats an offline score as a **candidate predictor**, not ground truth, and a rollout as an **intervention**, not a larger validation set. It does not promise that all production outcomes are observable, that observational adjustment removes unmeasured confounding, that shadow output estimates human behavior under exposure, or that one organization's cohort generalizes to all Headlamp users.

#### Separate construct, prediction, decision, and impact claims

Use a claim ladder. Passing a lower level is necessary but does not establish the next:

| Level | Claim                                                                                           | Minimum evidence                                                                                                                           |
| ----- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| 0     | **Technical validity:** the intended candidate, environment, metric, and deployment were logged | Closed Topic 17/19 manifests; linkage and telemetry controls; no silent version mixing                                                     |
| 1     | **Construct validity:** the offline metric measures its named capability                        | Topic 4-6 expert gold, grader calibration, hard state/evidence checks, and known-good/known-bad controls                                   |
| 2     | **Predictive validity:** a frozen score predicts a later target outcome                         | Prospective temporal/external cohort; prespecified unit, horizon, model and metrics; discrimination, calibration, coverage and uncertainty |
| 3     | **Decision utility:** using the prediction at a threshold has acceptable benefit/harm tradeoffs | Prespecified action policy and loss/utility; threshold-specific false-action, missed-action, abstention and capacity consequences          |
| 4     | **Impact validity:** exposing operators or systems to the candidate changes outcomes            | Randomized/staged intervention where feasible, or an explicit target-trial/quasi-experimental design with falsification/sensitivity tests  |
| 5     | **Transport and durability:** claims hold in target cohorts and remain current                  | Site/time/cohort validation, shift and missingness analysis, negative controls, expiry/revalidation policy                                 |

TRIPOD distinguishes model development/internal validation from validation on other participant data and warns that apparent performance on development data is optimistic [R21-4](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.g7594). It also explicitly does not cover impact studies. That medical reporting framework is used here only as a mature methodological analogy: Topic 21 must separately validate prediction and intervention impact.

An offline aggregate cannot directly predict an individual incident unless a mapping is defined. Avoid ecological claims such as “release $C_1$ scored five points higher, therefore each production session is five points safer.” Define one or more frozen deployment prediction functions:

$$
\hat p_{m,v}(Y_{i,h}=1\mid X_i,C,E)=f_{m,v}(S_{C,E},X_i),
$$

where $m,v$ identify the metric and prediction-rule version, $S_{C,E}$ is the offline evidence for candidate $C$ in environment $E$, $X_i$ contains only features available at prediction time, and $Y_{i,h}$ is one adjudicated outcome within horizon $h$. Every claim names its prediction time, unit, horizon, eligibility rules, and intended decision.

Bind each probability to exactly one event definition and horizon. “Probability of safe escalation judgment within seven days” and “probability of sustained incident resolution within 24 hours” are different prediction targets with separate calibration evidence; one score cannot be calibrated against the entire outcome table at once.

#### Prospective validation record and leakage control

Freeze a study protocol and signed validation record before the first target outcome is examined:

`study_id, protocol_revision, claim_id, metric_version, prediction_rule_digest, candidate/environment manifests, target population, eligible unit, index time, prediction horizon, outcome definitions, covariates, strata, exposure arms, allocation mechanism/propensities, analysis set, estimands, practical margins, alpha/interval policy, multiplicity family, sample/information target, stopping rule, missingness plan, censoring/competing events, privacy basis, linkage method, retention, adjudication plan, negative controls, shift gates, analysis code digest`.

Name one primary metric-outcome-horizon-policy contrast for each confirmatory study. Freeze a gatekeeping or multiplicity policy over all other confirmatory contrasts and label secondary, subgroup, and exploratory analyses as such; selecting the best metric, horizon, threshold, or baseline after outcomes are known creates a new development result, not validation.

Preserve prediction records append-only:

`prediction_id, study_id, eligible_unit_id, cohort/site/time block, metric inputs and versions, predicted probability/risk tier, abstention, candidate policy, baseline policy, assignment, actual exposure received, environment manifest, prediction timestamp`.

Outcome adjudicators should not see candidate identity, offline score, predicted tier, or desired launch outcome where practical. Separate the team maintaining offline metrics from the team finalizing production labels. Cases used to redesign a metric move into development data and cannot remain untouched external validation. Model Cards recommend reporting intended use, evaluation conditions, subgroups and limitations [R21-25](https://doi.org/10.1145/3287560.3287596); Datasheets similarly systematize dataset motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing, uses, distribution and maintenance [R21-26](https://doi.org/10.1145/3458723). Neither artifact is evidence that its contents are true, so bind claims to executable manifests and audits.

#### Outcome contract

Define outcomes independently of assistant phrasing and before linkage. Keep component outcomes separate; do not create one “production quality” score whose weights can hide harm.

| Outcome                  | Eligible unit and index                                                 | Positive/negative event and censoring                                                                                                       | Key confounders or measurement threats                                                                   |
| ------------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Expert judgment          | Privacy-reviewed sampled session/trajectory at final assistant output   | Blinded rubric facts, evidence, safety, action appropriateness and uncertainty; disagreement retained                                       | Reviewer calibration, incomplete cluster evidence, style/model identity leakage, selective review        |
| Support resolution       | New support case linked before candidate exposure                       | Prespecified resolved state, reopen/escalation within horizon, and verified task outcome; unresolved is censored, not failure or success    | Case severity, support staffing, customer responsiveness, duplicate/merged tickets, channel exclusion    |
| Safe escalation          | Session reaches a prespecified uncertainty/risk decision point          | Correct escalate/abstain/continue decision against later adjudication; include false escalation and unsafe non-escalation                   | Escalation capacity, user refusal, missing later truth, policy/version changes                           |
| Incident duration        | Incident declaration under a stable incident-definition policy          | Time to independently verified mitigation and time to sustained resolution as separate endpoints                                            | Left truncation, right censoring, severity, concurrent responders, changing declaration/closure practice |
| Rollback                 | Candidate/version exposure begins                                       | Product rollback, action compensation and unrelated deployment rollback are distinct; reason and causal review required                     | Precautionary rollbacks, bundled releases, automated rollback criteria, repeated exposure                |
| Production failure class | Eligible exposed or shadowed unit with sufficient observability         | Prespecified taxonomy: wrong RCA, unsupported claim, unsafe action, tool/runtime, concurrency, ecosystem, measurement, privacy, or no fault | Detection/reporting propensity, changed taxonomy, duplicate incidents, unknown denominator               |
| Cluster/system outcome   | Candidate-visible action or recommendation with declared affected scope | Verified recovery, safety invariant, collateral change, recurrence and sustained window                                                     | Controllers, human changes, unrelated deploys, workload demand, shared-cluster interference              |
| Operator workflow        | Consenting task/session                                                 | Time to safe decision, evidence inspection, correction, override, abandonment and handoff; satisfaction remains secondary                   | Expertise, workload, novelty, learning/carryover, Hawthorne effect, UI/version differences               |

Google SRE incident guidance defines distinct incident roles, a live incident state and explicit handoff, illustrating why incident outcomes require stable process definitions [R21-27](https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/). Use organization-owned definitions and record changes; do not infer “resolved” from chat ending, ticket closure alone, a Kubernetes status snapshot, or absence of a report.

For incident duration, prespecify the time origin, independently verified mitigation/resolution event, sustained window, observation horizon, and the disposition of every non-resolution event. Report unresolved cases as right-censored only when independent censoring is defensible rather than dropping them or replacing duration with the observation window. Kaplan and Meier formalized nonparametric estimation from incomplete observations [R21-22](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1958.10501452). Classify rollback, escalation, abandonment, environment retirement, and closure without verified resolution as failure, competing event, or censoring according to the estimand and causal ordering fixed in the protocol; those labels are not interchangeable. When an event genuinely precludes target resolution, estimate the relevant cumulative-incidence function or use another prespecified competing-risk analysis; Fine and Gray provide one subdistribution model [R21-23](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1999.10474144). These methods require censoring/model assumptions and do not repair inconsistent incident labels.

#### Predictive validation: more than correlation

Run temporal validation first, then external validation across at least one meaningful boundary such as organization/site, cluster distribution, operator expertise, incident family, provider, or language/accessibility stratum. Keep the prediction rule fixed during each cohort. Report:

- cohort flow from eligible to instrumented, predicted, linked, labeled and analyzed;
- prevalence/base rate and outcome delay;
- discrimination appropriate to the endpoint, with uncertainty;
- calibration-in-the-large, calibration slope, flexible calibration curve and proper scoring rule for probabilities;
- sensitivity/specificity or recall/precision at every policy threshold, plus abstention/coverage;
- subgroup estimates and interaction uncertainty, not only pooled performance;
- comparison with production policy, incident severity alone, operator-only judgment, and simple baselines;
- incremental value over those baselines, not merely univariate score-outcome correlation;
- practical decision consequences and capacity at proposed thresholds.

Calibration asks whether observed frequencies agree with predicted probabilities. A predictor can rank well while systematically overstating safety; validation therefore needs sufficiently large samples and calibration curves [R21-5](https://doi.org/10.1186/s12916-019-1466-7). Do not call a raw 0-100 rubric score a 90% success probability unless a separately frozen calibration model supports that interpretation.

Decision-curve analysis demonstrates one way to express threshold-specific net benefit from false-positive/false-negative tradeoffs [R21-6](https://doi.org/10.1177/0272989X06295361). For Headlamp, publish the actual utility table instead of importing clinical assumptions. Hard safety failures remain vetoes; they cannot be offset by faster resolution. Decision utility also depends on review/escalation capacity, so a threshold valid for a five-case pilot may fail under full traffic.

Empirical recommender work confirms that offline-online alignment is a study question, not an axiom. Swissinfo work compared offline and online news recommendation [R21-17](https://doi.org/10.1145/2645710.2645745); later work sought richer offline metrics that predict online news performance [R21-18](https://doi.org/10.1145/2792838.2800184); an Indeed study evaluated prediction of online job-recommender performance from offline evaluation [R21-19](https://doi.org/10.1145/3298689.3347032). These are small, domain-specific recommender studies, not evidence that any Kubernetes metric is predictive. Their value is demonstrating that candidate offline metrics can be compared against accumulated online experiments and selected empirically rather than assumed aligned.

#### Shadow mode validates predictions, not treatment effects

In **shadow mode**, the production workflow determines user-visible actions while the candidate receives the same eligible input and emits a sealed recommendation/trajectory. Shadowing can test technical compatibility, coverage, latency, disagreement, prospective expert labels, and whether a frozen score predicts later outcomes under the **baseline** policy. It cannot measure how users would rely on the candidate, whether its actions would change cluster state, or the outcome under the candidate policy.

Human Decisions and Machine Predictions illustrates the selective-label problem: outcomes were visible only for defendants released under prior human decisions, so comparing a new policy required explicit counterfactual strategies and quasi-random assignment [R21-24](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjx032). In this framework, production actions similarly determine which diagnoses, remediations, and failures become observable. Never fill an unobserved candidate outcome with the baseline outcome and call it a paired comparison.

For passive/off-policy estimates, log the baseline action space, chosen action, probability of that action under the logging policy, candidate action, context available to both policies, and delayed reward. The contextual-bandit replay method gives unbiased offline evaluation under randomized logging and overlap/support assumptions [R21-20](https://doi.org/10.1145/1935826.1935878). Deterministic operator policies, hidden context, near-zero propensity, compound multi-turn actions, safety filtering, and interference can make the estimand unidentified or estimates unusably variable. Never introduce unsafe exploration merely to satisfy positivity; mark unsupported actions and use staged expert/sandbox evaluation.

#### Staged impact studies

Move from prediction to impact only after Topic 7 safety, Topic 18 integrity, Topic 19 compatibility, Topic 20 concurrency, and the lower validity levels pass. Recommended sequence:

1. **Retrospective exploration:** discover candidate outcomes and confounders; generate hypotheses only.
2. **Prospective shadow:** freeze predictions and labels before outcomes; no user-visible candidate action.
3. **Paired expert simulation:** candidate/baseline trajectories on replayable or ephemeral clusters with blinded adjudication.
4. **Internal supervised pilot:** consenting trained operators; recommendations visible, mutation disabled or separately approved; rapid stop rules.
5. **Randomized canary:** assign at the smallest unit that prevents contamination, with an immutable baseline arm and intention-to-treat analysis.
6. **Cluster or stepped rollout:** randomize organization/team/cluster/time blocks when users share knowledge or workflows; model period and cluster effects.
7. **Monitored adoption:** continue controls/sentinels, shift monitoring, incident linkage, and periodic external revalidation.

Define impact estimands before assignment. For a binary safe-resolution outcome under assigned candidate policy $Z$:

$$
\operatorname{ITT}=E[Y_i\mid Z_i=1]-E[Y_i\mid Z_i=0].
$$

Use intention-to-treat as primary because actual exposure, override and noncompliance are consequences of deployment. Report treatment received, reliance and crossover descriptively; per-protocol or complier effects need additional assumptions. Randomization unit, analysis unit and uncertainty must agree. Sessions from one operator, incidents in one cluster, repeated organization exposures and related scenario families are not independent.

Define $Z$ as assignment to a complete policy over a fixed investigation window, not as whichever assistant produced the last message. Before enrollment, freeze the index event, policy availability, candidate/baseline versions, follow-up, whether opposite-arm access is blocked, and how multi-turn advice, viewing, reliance, override and crossover are logged. Choose the randomization unit only after mapping shared operators, clusters, teams and communication channels; if knowledge can cross session arms, randomize a higher-level operator/team/cluster/time block and analyze that dependence. Keep post-assignment reliance and switching out of the primary total-effect adjustment set. An adaptive sequence of changing policies requires a separately identified dynamic-regime estimand, not the single-assignment ITT above.

The stepped-wedge design staggers cluster crossover while accounting for secular time, but all clusters eventually receive the intervention and analysis must model period/cluster structure [R21-11](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.h391). Use it only when delayed rollout is acceptable and equipoise remains. Overlapping experiment infrastructure can increase experimentation capacity while managing interactions [R21-12](https://doi.org/10.1145/1835804.1835810), but Headlamp must explicitly record concurrent experiments and test interactions; orthogonal bucket labels do not prove absence of interference.

Prespecify guardrails and stop rules for secret exposure, destructive action, severe wrong-cluster mutation, lost update, unsafe non-escalation, privilege expansion, outage, and privacy failure. Safety stopping is not optional-hypothesis peeking. Efficacy/futility looks need a sequential design or alpha policy fixed before data. Preserve stopped cohorts and reasons; do not delete a harmful arm from later summaries.

#### Observational and quasi-experimental evidence

Randomization can be infeasible for emergency fixes, organization-wide changes, low-frequency severe incidents, or opt-in features. Before analyzing observational exposure, emulate a target trial: eligibility, treatment strategies, assignment time, follow-up, outcomes, causal contrast, and analysis [R21-8](https://doi.org/10.1093/aje/kwv254). Avoid immortal-time bias by assigning exposure at a clear index; do not classify an incident as “candidate-assisted” because the assistant was opened only after a long unsuccessful baseline period.

Adjustment using propensity scores balances **observed** pretreatment covariates under strong assumptions [R21-9](https://doi.org/10.1093/biomet/70.1.41). Record severity, incident family, cluster/environment, operator expertise/workload, site, provider, time, prior assistant use, staffing and concurrent changes. Before outcomes, freeze the pretreatment covariate set, propensity/weighting model, overlap diagnostic, unsupported-region rule, balance criterion and sensitivity analyses. Report excluded target regions rather than silently trimming them. Never write “caused” from adjusted observational data without no-unmeasured-confounding, consistency, positivity and interference assumptions.

Interrupted time series can estimate level/slope changes when a rollout has enough stable pre/post points, models autocorrelation/seasonality, and lacks coincident changes [R21-10](https://doi.org/10.1093/ije/dyw098). Prefer a concurrent control series. Bundled Headlamp, model, policy, staffing, Kubernetes, or support-process changes prevent assigning the effect to the assistant unless separately identified.

Transporting results across sites requires explicit knowledge of how populations, regimes and sampling differ; data-fusion methods formalize when heterogeneous data can identify a target causal query [R21-21](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1510507113). In practice, publish target-versus-study differences and avoid extrapolation when key effect modifiers or selection mechanisms are unmeasured.

#### Missing populations, selective labels, and linkage

For every cohort publish the flow:

$$
N_{eligible}\rightarrow N_{instrumented}\rightarrow N_{assigned}\rightarrow N_{exposed}\rightarrow N_{linkable}\rightarrow N_{labelled}\rightarrow N_{analysed}.
$$

Stratify reasons at each transition: telemetry disabled; privacy/legal exclusion; unsupported provider or cluster; offline/no-network use; session abandoned; no incident ID; support channel unavailable; outcome not yet mature; ticket merged; audit/trace incomplete; user opted out; organization left; or label adjudication failed. Retain counts without retaining sensitive content where possible.

Missingness threats include:

- **coverage bias:** only instrumented online deployments appear, excluding air-gapped, CLI, self-hosted or privacy-sensitive users;
- **reporting bias:** obvious failures generate tickets while silent wrong advice and successful unassisted work do not;
- **selective labels:** production policy determines which recommendation/action outcome is observed;
- **informative censoring:** difficult incidents remain open, customers disengage, or telemetry retention expires;
- **linkage error:** one session maps to several incidents or a support case merges users/releases;
- **survivorship:** rolled-back versions have short exposure and successful long-lived versions accumulate more observations;
- **consent and language/accessibility gaps:** populations most affected may be least likely to produce linkable feedback.

STROBE requires transparent participant selection, variables, bias, study size, missing data, sensitivity analysis and generalisability reporting for observational studies [R21-7](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj.39335.541782.AD). It is a reporting guideline, not a cure for bias. Use inverse-probability weighting or multiple imputation only with recorded predictors and defensible missing-at-random/positivity assumptions; report complete-case and sensitivity bounds. Do not impute severe unobserved outcomes from satisfaction, ticket absence, chat completion, or the assistant's own confidence.

#### Distribution shift and failure-class coverage

Monitor four separate changes between offline, shadow and live cohorts:

1. $P(X)$: operator, incident, Kubernetes/operator/provider, language, permission, scale and telemetry mix;
2. $P(Y)$: outcome prevalence and label/adjudication policy;
3. $P(Y\mid X)$: relationship between predictors and outcome, including changed workflows or controller behavior;
4. $P(A\mid X)$: operator/system action and exposure policy, including reliance and escalation.

Dataset-shift taxonomies distinguish covariate, prior-probability and concept changes under different assumptions [R21-15](https://doi.org/10.1016/j.patcog.2011.06.019). Empirical work shows two-sample and domain-classifier methods can detect some shifts [R21-16](https://papers.nips.cc/paper/2019/hash/846c260d715e5b854ffad5f70a516c88-Abstract.html). An unlabeled input-shift alarm neither proves harm nor excludes concept shift. Pair shift tests with sentinel labels, calibration/outcome monitoring and root-cause review; control repeated-testing false alarms and report detection power for reference shifts.

Maintain a production-to-offline taxonomy matrix with weighted and unweighted counts:

| Production class                       | Offline exact/analog coverage | Shadow detection | Label completeness | Action                                                                  |
| -------------------------------------- | ----------------------------- | ---------------- | ------------------ | ----------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Covered and stable                     | Named scenario lineage        | Expected         | Adequate           | Continue sentinel and periodic revalidation                             |
| Covered but frequency/severity shifted | Existing family               | Changed          | Adequate           | Reweight only with a frozen target estimand; add representative cases   |
| New valid failure                      | None                          | Detected         | Reviewed           | Quarantine claim slice, create provenance-reviewed holdout then promote |
| Interface/environment incompatibility  | Topic 19 cell                 | Detected         | Adequate           | Fix compatibility; do not label reasoning regression                    |
| Unobservable or privacy-excluded       | Unknown                       | Unknown          | Inadequate         | Narrow claim and report missing population                              |
| Measurement/taxonomy drift             | Nominal match                 | Changed          | Invalid            | Version labels/metric; bridge or stop trend                             |

Do not immediately train on every production failure. Preserve an untouched temporal external-validation stream, deduplicate incident families, scan for contamination under Topic 18, and promote cases through Topic 1 provenance and Topic 4 expert review.

#### Metric governance: recalibrate, revise, suspend, or retire

Each metric/claim pair has an append-only lifecycle:

`proposed -> internally-qualified -> prospectively-validating -> deployment-validated -> monitoring -> degraded -> suspended -> retired`.

Decisions are claim-specific. A metric can remain useful for offline diagnosis while losing rollout-gating validity. Apply these rules:

| Evidence state                                                                                     | Decision                                                                                               |
| -------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Ranking remains useful; calibration intercept/slope drifts with adequate labels                    | Recalibrate as a new prediction-rule version; prospectively validate; preserve old predictions/results |
| Construct unchanged but feature/metric mapping changes                                             | Revise metric version and run a temporal bridge; do not splice series                                  |
| Offline delta improves but prospective discrimination/calibration or live guardrails do not        | Remove from rollout benefit claims; retain as diagnostic only if construct validity remains            |
| Predictive validity passes but randomized/staged impact is null or harmful                         | Do not claim deployment benefit; inspect workflow, reliance, threshold and intervention fidelity       |
| Severe escaped failure, privacy breach, invalid grader, contamination, or unresolved label drift   | Suspend affected claim/gate immediately pending independent review                                     |
| Coverage below floor, key cohort lacks overlap, confidence too wide, or shift detector fires alone | Mark inconclusive/degraded; narrow target population or collect approved evidence, not “pass”          |
| Repeated external/impact failure, construct no longer decision-relevant, or no maintainable labels | Retire from release policy with replacement/lineage and historical report retained                     |

Do not select the best-correlating metric and report its same-data correlation. Divide studies into metric-development, calibration, temporal validation and external/impact cohorts; account for the prespecified multiplicity family under Topic 10. Google guidance explicitly says utilitarian performance can matter more than predictive power and that an objective should be revisited when its optimized metric improves while system performance degrades [R21-13](https://developers.google.com/machine-learning/guides/rules-of-ml).

#### Privacy, security, and study governance

Production validity does not authorize broad prompt, cluster, identity, or support-data collection. NIST's Privacy Framework treats privacy as enterprise risk management [R21-3](https://www.nist.gov/privacy-framework), while the AI RMF and GenAI profile place measurement and monitoring inside governed lifecycle risk management [R21-1](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.100-1), [R21-2](https://doi.org/10.6028/NIST.AI.600-1). Before instrumentation, require privacy, security, legal and affected-stakeholder review appropriate to deployment.

The study data contract should specify purpose, lawful/organizational basis, notice/consent where required, eligible populations, data minimization, prohibited fields, redaction at source, linkage custodian, pseudonym rotation, access roles, geographic boundary, encryption, retention/deletion, incident response, withdrawal/deletion handling, aggregation thresholds, publication review and secondary-use prohibition. Enforce an allowlisted derived event/fact schema and one-way study linkage at the collection boundary: reject or quarantine unknown/prohibited fields, test redaction and deletion, and block pilot enrollment until privacy/security review approves the schema. Raw prompts, Kubernetes objects, secrets, logs, names and support text must not enter the analysis path merely because policy says they should not.

Separate operational identity from study identity. A restricted linkage service can map short-lived product/session/incident IDs to study IDs and then discard or escrow the mapping according to policy. The analysis dataset receives cohort, exposure, outcome and approved covariates, not credentials or direct identifiers. Privacy exclusions change the target population and must appear in flow/transport analyses; privacy-preserving collection is not statistically ignorable by declaration.

Shadow candidates must receive no broader data or permissions than the production path and must not cause external side effects, user-visible output, cache pollution, quota starvation, or model-provider retention outside the approved contract. Topic 18 leakage controls apply: production outcomes and support labels must not become candidate-visible benchmark answers.

#### Failure ownership and invalidity

Preserve the first invalidating layer:

- `prediction_identity_failure`: score, prediction rule, candidate, environment or horizon was not frozen/resolvable;
- `eligibility_or_assignment_failure`: cohort entry, randomization/bucketing, propensity or concurrent experiment was wrong;
- `exposure_failure`: assigned policy was not delivered, shadow affected production, or treatment versions mixed;
- `linkage_failure`: prediction cannot be unambiguously joined to the eligible outcome unit;
- `outcome_measurement_failure`: label definition, adjudication, censoring, audit or evidence is incomplete/changed;
- `privacy_governance_failure`: collection, access, retention, deletion or use exceeds the approved contract;
- `positivity_or_transport_failure`: target cohort/action has no supported comparison or measured bridge;
- `analysis_failure`: leakage, post-treatment adjustment, dependence, multiplicity, time trend or missingness was mishandled;
- `predictive_validity_failure`: eligible study is complete but discrimination, calibration, coverage or practical threshold fails;
- `impact_validity_failure`: eligible intervention study shows null, inconclusive, or harmful effect under its prespecified rule.

Null and inconclusive are not implementation failures. Report them. A harmful impact result can coexist with accurate prediction if the workflow changes behavior badly; a beneficial randomized result can coexist with poor score calibration if exposure helps through another mechanism. Do not rewrite either into the preferred narrative.

#### Known-invalid designs and interpretations

Reject designs or claims that:

- correlate one release-level offline score with a handful of incidents and call it individual predictive validity;
- tune metric weights, thresholds, labels, strata, horizons or exclusions after seeing deployment outcomes and report confirmatory inference;
- treat internal cross-validation, a reused benchmark, or retrospective production fitting as external validation;
- call AUC/rank correlation calibration, or call calibration proof that thresholded actions benefit users;
- infer impact from shadow mode, since candidate output did not alter operator action or cluster state;
- assign baseline outcomes to unexecuted shadow actions or compare only cases where candidate and baseline agree;
- treat ticket closure, thumbs-up, chat completion, absence of rollback, or absence of a report as verified safe resolution;
- drop unresolved incidents, candidate rollbacks, telemetry opt-outs, unlinked sessions, failed adjudications or unsupported populations from denominators;
- compare raw mean incident duration without severity, clustering, censoring, competing events and stable start/end definitions;
- adjust for post-exposure variables such as operator reliance, candidate-driven escalation, tool calls or early response when estimating total impact;
- use propensity weighting without measured confounders, overlap, balance diagnostics and sensitivity analysis;
- use interrupted time series with too few points or a coincident model/UI/Kubernetes/support-policy rollout and attribute the bundle to one component;
- randomize sessions when operators share recommendations across arms, or ignore repeated operator/cluster/organization dependence;
- stop an experiment for benefit after repeated unplanned looks and use a fixed-sample p-value;
- average safety, speed, cost, satisfaction and resolution into one score that permits serious harm to be offset;
- call detected covariate shift performance degradation, or call no detected input shift proof of stable performance;
- reweight to a target population with zero/near-zero overlap or unmeasured selection, or generalize beyond consented/instrumented cohorts silently;
- mine support text or cluster traces before purpose, minimization, retention, access, redaction and deletion governance is approved;
- train immediately on validation/production failures and continue reporting the same cohort as untouched external evidence;
- keep a metric in a release gate because retiring it would break the historical trend after it stops predicting decision-relevant outcomes.

#### Local implementation implications

The current repository does not yet provide the linkage needed for Topic 21:

- [e2e/README.md](../e2e/README.md) describes a local Headlamp/KWOK/Playwright suite with screenshots and scripted/fixture-backed interactions. It supplies product wiring evidence, not production exposure, operator, incident, support, rollback or outcome cohorts.
- [conversation/types.ts](../packages/ai-common/src/conversation/types.ts) records role/content, tool-call/request IDs, UI activity timestamps and approval callbacks. It has no release/study/cohort/assignment, consent/privacy, candidate/environment manifest, prediction, exposure, incident/support, adjudication, outcome or retention identity.
- [ProactiveDiagnosisManager.ts](../packages/ai-ui/src/diagnosis/ProactiveDiagnosisManager.ts) caches generated diagnoses in process by Kubernetes Event UID and keeps event content, diagnosis text, timestamps, errors and thinking steps. It deduplicates later events by a normalized resource key. This is useful UI state, but it is not a durable study record, verified outcome, random sample, privacy-reviewed linkage, or exposure log. Its open `rawEvent` record can contain names, messages, or other cluster-derived content, so it is ineligible for direct reuse as the allowlisted study envelope.
- No repository path matching a canonical eval result schema, production feedback schema, shadow assignment, support/incident join or rollout outcome registry was found in the inspected plugin snapshot. Topic 10's proposed production loop therefore remains a design, not current implementation evidence.

Do not add raw production prompts as the first implementation step. First define the privacy-reviewed minimal study/event schema, generate synthetic records, and prove linkage, deletion, invalidity and cohort-flow accounting offline. Then instrument technical exposure identities without content. Only after governance approval should a bounded pilot collect approved production-derived labels.

#### Focused pilot

1. Write and preregister a machine-readable protocol for one narrow primary claim: whether a frozen offline safe-escalation score predicts blinded expert safe-escalation judgment for read-only pod diagnosis within seven days. Define one event/horizon, index and end states, unit, cohort, labels, strata, practical margins, named always/never-escalate and severity-only baselines, multiplicity family, missingness, and any sequential stopping policy before outcomes.
2. Implement synthetic versioned `study`, `prediction`, `assignment`, `exposure`, `linkage`, `outcome`, `adjudication`, `shift`, and `metric-decision` schemas. Test referential integrity, append-only corrections, retention/deletion, role access, and reconstruction of every cohort-flow count.
3. Add a content-free exposure envelope to local E2E: candidate/environment digests, prediction/assignment/exposure IDs, mode (`offline|shadow|visible|actionable`), timestamps and invalidity. Prove no raw prompt, cluster object, secret, user or support identifier is emitted.
4. Run a retrospective feasibility study only to estimate prevalence, label delay, cluster/operator dependence, missingness, review capacity and sample/information needs. Lock its unit IDs and time window, mark every discovered association exploratory, and begin confirmation in a later disjoint prospective cohort.
5. Run a prospective shadow cohort against the same production-visible inputs where policy permits. Seal candidate output before the baseline outcome, sample baseline-only and disagreement cases with known probabilities, and send both through blinded expert adjudication. Report weighted and unweighted estimates.
6. Validate the frozen predictor: discrimination, calibration curve/intercept/slope, proper score, threshold confusion/coverage, incremental value over severity and baseline, and prespecified incident/operator/environment slices. Include bootstrap or clustered intervals appropriate to the sampling unit.
7. Inject measurement controls: changed label rubric, missing high-severity cases, delayed unresolved outcomes, false linkage, candidate version mixing, telemetry opt-out, and an uninstrumented cohort. Require the pipeline to invalidate or narrow the claim rather than silently complete data.
8. Inject reference distribution shifts in Kubernetes version, provider, incident family, expertise, language and permissions. Measure detector false alarms/power; prove a shift alarm triggers review but does not itself declare quality loss.
9. If predictive and privacy gates pass, run a consenting internal randomized recommendation-only canary with mutation disabled. Before enrollment, map contamination paths and freeze one operator/team/cluster/time-block randomization unit, blocking/stratification factors, and a full-investigation candidate-versus-baseline availability policy. Log recommendation view, reliance, override and crossover without adjusting the primary intention-to-treat effect for those post-assignment variables. Prespecify safe escalation, time to verified diagnosis, a minimum practical benefit margin, and hard safety guardrails.
10. Simulate noncompliance, crossover, shared operator learning, concurrent UI/model release, response censoring and early safety stop. Require correct estimand, clustering, period adjustment, competing-event treatment and preserved stopped-arm records.
11. Compare offline delta, shadow predictive results and randomized impact. Exercise four governance outcomes: deployment-validated only after the impact margin passes, recalibrated after predictive drift, diagnostic-only after null/inconclusive impact, and suspended after harm or a severe escaped failure. Null or inconclusive impact is a no-rollout result for the deployment-benefit claim even when retaining the metric diagnostically. Preserve metric versions and historical decisions.
12. Promote one privacy-reviewed production failure into a new scenario through Topic 1/4/18 controls while retaining a separate untouched temporal stream. Verify that no candidate can read the production label or new holdout gold.

Separate framework execution from empirical claims. The framework pilot succeeds only if candidate/environment/exposure identity is closed; the target cohort and losses are enumerable; outcomes are independent and blinded; privacy controls reject raw sensitive collection; injected missingness, shift, linkage and version errors invalidate or narrow results; and the prewritten governance rule is executed even when unfavorable. The predictive claim passes only when its prespecified prospective margins pass. The deployment-benefit claim passes only when the eligible intention-to-treat estimate meets its practical benefit margin without a hard-guardrail violation; null, harmful, or inconclusive impact cannot justify rollout, although correctly recording that result demonstrates the framework. A significant retrospective correlation or an offline gain followed by unchanged deployment outcomes is not empirical success.

#### Counterevidence and limitations

- Offline metrics can be valuable without predicting every production endpoint: deterministic safety invariants, schema conformance and rare catastrophic controls can remain release gates on construct/risk grounds. Topic 21 must name that rationale rather than mislabeling it empirical predictive validity.
- Production outcomes are jointly caused by operator, assistant, tools, cluster, organization and incident. Weak candidate effects may require more information than a practical safe pilot can collect; an inconclusive study is not evidence of equivalence.
- Randomized trials may exclude rare high-risk groups, alter behavior, or be unethical for destructive actions. Sandbox/expert evidence and hard safety policy remain necessary even after a benign canary.
- Shadow evaluation avoids direct treatment risk but cannot observe reliance, action consequences, feedback loops, or candidate-induced data. It can overestimate validity when candidate outputs would change future inputs.
- Recommender, clinical and web-experiment studies provide methods and mismatch examples, not effect sizes or guaranteed best practices for Kubernetes operations.
- Labeling production RCA and safe action is expensive and sometimes impossible after evidence expires. Review capacity and retention limits constrain attainable precision and may force narrower claims.
- Privacy minimization can reduce linkage and subgroup visibility. The solution is not unlimited collection; report the resulting target-population boundary and seek safer aggregate or prospective study designs.
- Dataset-shift tests have finite power and repeated alarms; concept drift can occur without detectable $P(X)$ change. Direct sentinel outcomes and calibration checks remain necessary.
- Metric governance creates feedback: teams may optimize validated metrics, operators may adapt reliance, and promoted incidents can contaminate benchmarks. Keep rotating holdouts, negative controls and periodic construct review.
- Cross-organization transport may be impossible when workflows, support definitions, incident severity or observability differ. Publish local validity rather than a universal Headlamp claim.

| [R21-19](https://doi.org/10.1145/3298689.3347032): Predicting Online Performance of Job Recommender Systems with Offline Evaluation            | Industrial study relating offline job-recommender evaluation to accumulated online performance                                              | Short, domain-specific study; unavailable outcome details and selection of experiments limit extrapolation                                  |
| [R21-20](https://doi.org/10.1145/1935826.1935878): Unbiased Offline Evaluation of Contextual-Bandit News Recommendation                        | Replay/off-policy evaluation from randomized logged actions under support and known logging-policy assumptions                              | Single-step news actions; variance/support, hidden context, multi-turn dependence, safety filtering and interference constrain Headlamp use |
| [R21-21](https://doi.org/10.1073/pnas.1510507113): Causal Inference and the Data-Fusion Problem                                                | Nonparametric framework for combining heterogeneous populations, regimes and samples under explicit causal structure                        | Identification requires correct selection/causal assumptions and measured bridge variables; not a license for arbitrary reweighting         |
| [R21-22](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1958.10501452): Nonparametric Estimation from Incomplete Observations                                | Kaplan-Meier product-limit estimation for time-to-event data with right-censored observations                                               | Requires appropriate censoring assumptions and consistent time origin/event; competing events need separate treatment                       |
| [R21-23](https://doi.org/10.1080/01621459.1999.10474144): A Proportional Hazards Model for the Subdistribution of a Competing Risk             | Fine-Gray regression for cumulative incidence/subdistribution hazards with competing events                                                 | Proportional/model assumptions and interpretation differ from causal effects; use only for prespecified incident competing events           |
| [R21-24](https://doi.org/10.1093/qje/qjx032): Human Decisions and Machine Predictions                                                          | Empirical/econometric study exposing selective labels, human-policy counterfactuals, broader utilities and quasi-random judge assignment    | Bail decision domain with specific instruments/preferences; methods and reported gains do not establish AI-agent benefit                    |
| [R21-25](https://doi.org/10.1145/3287560.3287596): Model Cards for Model Reporting                                                             | Documentation proposal for intended use, factors, metrics, evaluation data, subgroup results, ethical considerations and caveats            | A card can be incomplete or wrong and is not prospective validation, causal evidence or enforcement                                         |
| [R21-26](https://doi.org/10.1145/3458723): Datasheets for Datasets                                                                             | Peer-reviewed documentation framework for dataset motivation, composition, collection, preprocessing, uses, distribution and maintenance    | Documentation cannot recover missing populations, remove contamination or prove labels/consent are valid                                    |
| [R21-27](https://sre.google/sre-book/managing-incidents/): Google SRE incident management                                                      | Practitioner definitions of incident roles, state documentation, communication and explicit handoff useful for stable outcome contracts     | One organization's process and older publication; not a universal incident definition or causal evaluation                                  |
| [R21-28](https://doi.org/10.1145/3290605.3300233): Guidelines for Human-AI Interaction                                                         | Peer-reviewed synthesis/validation of human-AI design guidance including expectation, feedback, correction, control and failure support     | Design guidelines do not prove reliance, safety or deployment impact for Headlamp; Topic 14 requires controlled user studies                |
| [R21-29](https://doi.org/10.1136/bmj-2024-082505): PROBAST+AI                                                                                  | Updated structured appraisal of prediction-model quality, risk of bias, applicability, fairness and algorithmic-bias considerations         | Healthcare-oriented appraisal tool; not a substitute for Headlamp protocol, external validation or impact evidence                          |
| [R21-30](https://www.strobe-statement.org/checklists/): STROBE checklists                                                                      | Accessible design-specific cohort, case-control and cross-sectional reporting checklists                                                    | Website/checklists may evolve and duplicate the journal article's reporting authority; checklist completion does not establish validity     |

### Research 22: certification, tutorial, learning, and practice sources

#### Research method, scope, and separation

This research is deliberately separate from Research 11. Certification curricula, tutorials, courses, labs, and practice exams can define coverage, seed independently authored scenarios, support retrieval, or reveal useful grader patterns. They are not incident datasets merely because they contain Kubernetes tasks. Their exercise and answer counts must not inflate the Research 11 benchmark inventory.

The source search was refreshed on September 6, 2026. Search families included `CKA curriculum`, `CKAD curriculum`, `CKS curriculum`, `KCNA curriculum`, `KCSA curriculum`, `Linux Foundation Kubernetes training labs`, `Kubernetes tutorial exercises`, `Kubernetes certification practice exam`, `CKA mock exam grader`, `CKAD assessment.json`, `CKS validation script`, `Killer.sh simulator`, `Killercoda Kubernetes scenarios`, and GitHub combinations of `questions`, `answers`, `setup`, `verification`, `grader`, `namespace`, and certification names. Official CNCF, Linux Foundation, Kubernetes, Killer.sh, GitHub repository/API, and publisher-controlled pages were preferred over search summaries.

Repositories were inspected statically at immutable revisions where available. The audit checked licenses, file trees, task and answer location, setup and cleanup, machine-verifiable outcomes, Kubernetes freshness, deprecated APIs, provenance, and exam-integrity claims. No downloaded lab, installer, repository script, assessment, or validator was executed. Searches that advertised “real questions,” recalled exam questions, dumps, copied simulator content, or commercial-course answers were classified and excluded without ingesting their substantive content.

The primary hypothesis is: **official curricula improve coverage design, but no reviewed learning or practice source is a ready-made clean evaluation holdout**. The cheapest falsification was to find one source combining current official scope, explicit production-compatible reuse rights, reproducible setup, deterministic grading, independent provenance, and answers hidden from candidate developers and models. None met all conditions. The strongest executable public candidate, CK-X, publishes questions, answers, setup, and validators together and restricts production/commercial use; official Killer.sh content is access-controlled and has no open reuse grant.

Use five independent qualification fields instead of one “usable” label:

| Field                | Question                                                                                                                                         |
| -------------------- | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------ |
| Authority            | Is the source an official coverage specification, official documentation, authorized simulator, independent exercise set, or unknown derivative? |
| Rights               | Does an explicit license permit the intended copying, adaptation, training, redistribution, and production evaluation use?                       |
| Freshness            | Which curriculum and Kubernetes versions are named, and do tasks depend on removed APIs, mutable images, charts, external services, or defaults? |
| Executability        | Are environment setup, fault state, task prompt, cleanup, time limit, and independent machine-verifiable outcomes present?                       |
| Exposure and lineage | Are prompts, solutions, validators, source dependencies, and relationships to official or third-party material known and separated?              |

#### Official certification coverage is a specification, not a question bank

The CNCF curriculum repository at immutable commit `f6c7667265fef850daaf93b4e19e919552c67d8c` contains current and historical curriculum artifacts [R22-1](https://github.com/cncf/curriculum/commit/f6c7667265fef850daaf93b4e19e919552c67d8c). Its README grants CC BY 4.0 or later for the curriculum, although the repository has no root `LICENSE` and GitHub reports no repository-level license. Attribute the curriculum and preserve that source-level license evidence rather than inferring rights from repository visibility.

As of the research snapshot, the repository includes `CKA_Curriculum_v1.35.pdf`, `CKAD_Curriculum_v1.35.pdf`, `CKS_Curriculum v1.34.pdf`, `KCNA_Curriculum.pdf`, and `KCSA Curriculum.pdf`, plus Markdown summaries and historical files. Several differently named historical PDFs share blob identities, so filename counts are not counts of independent curricula. The Linux Foundation FAQ states that the live CKA, CKAD, and CKS environments use Kubernetes v1.35 [R22-7](https://docs.linuxfoundation.org/tc-docs/certification/faq-cka-ckad-cks). Curriculum artifact version and exam-environment version must therefore be recorded separately.

| Certification | Format in the official source | Published domains and weights                                                                                                                                                                             | Framework use                                                                                                                                               |
| ------------- | ----------------------------- | --------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ----------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| CKA           | Two-hour performance exam     | Cluster Architecture, Installation and Configuration 25%; Workloads and Scheduling 15%; Services and Networking 20%; Storage 10%; Troubleshooting 30%                                                     | Primary cluster-administration and troubleshooting coverage prior; it does not supply incident families, prompts, gold RCA, or grader instances             |
| CKAD          | Two-hour performance exam     | Application Design and Build 20%; Application Deployment 20%; Application Observability and Maintenance 15%; Application Environment, Configuration and Security 25%; Services and Networking 20%         | Application lifecycle and mutation-task coverage prior; add diagnosis, ambiguity, safety, evidence grounding, and operator workflows beyond exam objectives |
| CKS           | Two-hour performance exam     | Cluster Setup 10%; Cluster Hardening 15%; System Hardening 15%; Minimize Microservice Vulnerabilities 20%; Supply Chain Security 20%; Monitoring, Logging and Runtime Security 20%                        | Security scenario taxonomy and hard-invariant source; do not infer authorization to reuse official questions, and independently verify tool/API freshness   |
| KCNA          | Multiple-choice exam          | Kubernetes Fundamentals 44%; Container Orchestration 28%; Cloud Native Application Delivery 16%; Cloud Native Architecture 12%                                                                            | Concept and retrieval coverage; unsuitable by itself as evidence of tool use, diagnosis, remediation, or state change                                       |
| KCSA          | Multiple-choice exam          | Overview of Cloud Native Security 14%; Kubernetes Cluster Component Security 22%; Kubernetes Security Fundamentals 22%; Kubernetes Threat Model 16%; Platform Security 16%; Compliance and Frameworks 10% | Security concepts, threat-model terminology, and misconception probes; not a substitute for executable security controls                                    |

Weights are coverage priors, not target benchmark percentages. Certification objectives intentionally emphasize exam-relevant skills and can omit Headlamp UI behavior, MCP tools, multi-turn clarification, operator CRDs, provider failures, production incident ambiguity, cost, accessibility, and human handoff. Preserve Research 3's operational taxonomy and report curriculum coverage as an additional projection.

Official Kubernetes debugging pages are especially useful as evidence dictionaries: they name Pods, Services, StatefulSets, init containers, termination messages, nodes, control-plane components, logs, conditions, events, resource pressure, partitions, storage loss, and operator error [R22-10](https://github.com/kubernetes/website/commit/079ac780d512ab01d905e65dc622bfe38b94e6da). They should inform rubric facts and candidate-visible retrieval snapshots. They should not become exact held-out prompts, because models and candidates may already retrieve or memorize them.

#### Practice exams and exercise sets

Practice material has four distinct roles:

1. **Authorized simulator:** available through a certification registration under the provider's terms; useful for individual preparation and high-level interface study, but not automatically reusable as a corpus.
2. **Original public exercise set:** potentially reusable under its explicit license, but public questions and solutions are contaminated as a clean holdout.
3. **Convertible executable lab:** contains setup and independent checks that can inform a new implementation after rights, provenance, freshness, and leakage review.
4. **Dump or reconstruction:** claimed real, recalled, leaked, copied, or reverse-engineered exam content; prohibited from ingestion, training, scenario authoring, or evaluation.

The CK-X audit also found correctness and maintenance warnings that prevent direct scoring. One CKA question describes Pod Security Admission but labels its concept and validator as Pod Security Policy; the repository includes a `q6_s1_validate_psp.sh` path even though PodSecurityPolicy was removed from Kubernetes in v1.25. Some assessment and validator numbering is inconsistent or duplicated, including multiple validators sharing the same subtask prefix. Images and charts include moving `latest` tags and external repositories. Treat every setup and validator as untrusted, review it independently, pin all dependencies, and run reference/known-bad controls before reusing the architecture.

#### Exam integrity, rights, and leakage controls

The Linux Foundation certification agreement classifies exam materials as confidential and proprietary and prohibits disclosure, publication, reproduction, transmission, derivative works, reverse engineering, memorized reconstruction, unauthorized question publication, and braindumps [R22-8](https://docs.linuxfoundation.org/tc-docs/certification/lf-cert-agreement). These restrictions apply independently of whether a third party later places claimed content in a public repository.

Apply these hard rules:

- never collect, quote, summarize, embed, transform, or train on sources claiming actual, leaked, recalled, reconstructed, or “100% real” exam questions or answers;
- never use copied Killer.sh, Linux Foundation course, commercial course, or proprietary answer content without explicit permission covering the intended use;
- do not infer authorization from a public GitHub repository, stars, forks, a permissive license badge, or the contributor's claim of educational intent; verify source-level provenance and rights;
- quarantine exact and near-duplicate public practice prompts, solutions, manifests, distinctive names, validator strings, and answer trajectories from private holdouts using normalized text, AST/object, command, image, and semantic similarity checks;
- keep source-derived training/retrieval and evaluation lineage disjoint. Public exercises may be a declared contaminated development set, never the evidence for an unseen-capability claim;
- place private prompts, golds, setup identities, validator details, and canaries outside candidate/model retrieval. A public validator is useful for architecture review but not hidden evidence;
- preserve attribution and license obligations for every adapted source. `no license` means no default permission to copy or adapt, not “free for research”;
- have legal or rights owners approve any nontrivial incorporation of access-controlled, BSL, GPL, mixed-license, or uncertain-provenance material before engineering conversion.

#### Converting learning material into original evaluation cases

Use source material as a coverage and design input, not as text to paraphrase. For each proposed case:

1. Record source IDs, immutable revisions, file paths, licenses, access terms, curriculum domains, and whether prompts, answers, setup, or validators were visible.
2. Write a new operational capability statement independent of source wording. Add a realistic incident state, evidence path, ambiguity or distractor, permitted actions, safety constraints, and Headlamp/MCP interaction that the source does not supply.
3. Build setup and cleanup from pinned first-party or explicitly licensed components. Prove the fault through an independent grader identity before candidate execution.
4. Create semantic and hard-state golds from authoritative cluster behavior. Do not copy a published answer or make one command sequence the only accepted solution.
5. Write hidden graders that test outcomes, evidence, scope, side effects, and safety. Run no-agent, known-bad, shortcut, unsafe-effective, and reference controls.
6. Test on the declared Kubernetes support matrix. Detect removed APIs, changing defaults, mutable images/charts, external network requirements, architecture assumptions, timing, and nondeterministic controllers.
7. Run contamination checks against all public source prompts, solutions, manifests, validators, repository names, distinctive object names, and likely model-training mirrors. Replace contaminated cases or label them development-only.
8. Obtain independent review for provenance, rights, current curriculum mapping, operational realism, difficulty, and grader validity. Only then assign a new private case ID and immutable lineage.

A certification-shaped task can still be valuable as a public development check. Label it `learning-derived-public`, expose its lineage, and evaluate only regression in tool wiring or grader operation. Claims about generalization require separately authored, access-controlled incident families whose facts and solutions were not derived from the practice source.

#### Recommended source roles

| Need                                 | Preferred source                                                                            | Use policy                                                                                                                                           |
| ------------------------------------ | ------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- | ---------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------------- |
| Coverage and weighting               | Versioned CNCF curricula and official certification pages                                   | Snapshot and attribute; use as one projection, not benchmark composition or evidence of task validity                                                |
| Candidate retrieval                  | Pinned official Kubernetes documentation and attributed CNCF glossary content               | Candidate-visible corpus with version and locale recorded; do not use the same passages as hidden answer evidence                                    |
| Workload and fixture seeds           | Reviewed current area of `kubernetes/examples`                                              | Pin images/manifests, add independent fault/setup/cleanup/golds, and exclude archived or unsupported examples unless intentionally testing history   |
| Beginner and security gap analysis   | Public LFS158/LFS260 outlines                                                               | Use topic metadata only unless permission covers access-controlled course content                                                                    |
| Public development exercises         | MIT-licensed CKAD exercises or independently verified original material                     | Attribute, update, and label contaminated; never present exact-task performance as private holdout evidence                                          |
| Grader and simulator architecture    | CK-X static schema, setup/validator separation, and UI design                               | Research/reference under BSL; do not deploy commercially or import content without permission; independently reimplement and validate original cases |
| Authorized personal exam preparation | Killer.sh through an eligible registration                                                  | Use under provider terms; do not copy or convert its content                                                                                         |
| Clean release evaluation             | Independently authored private Headlamp incident scenarios with hidden graders and canaries | No practice-exam or course-answer derivation; enforce Topic 18 access, leakage, lineage, invalidation, and rotation controls                         |

#### Focused pilot

1. Import the five current curriculum files as versioned metadata only. Record artifact hash, curriculum version, domain weights, license evidence, and the separate official exam-environment version.
2. Add a coverage projection from every existing scenario to zero or more CKA, CKAD, CKS, KCNA, and KCSA domains. Review multi-label mappings and report unsupported Headlamp-specific dimensions alongside them.
3. Build a licensed retrieval snapshot from the Kubernetes documentation commit and selected CNCF glossary files. Preserve attribution, locale, source path, commit, and candidate-visible status; test one stale-page and one wrong-version retrieval control.
4. Convert one Apache-2.0 Kubernetes example into a newly authored read-only diagnosis case. Pin dependencies, inject an original fault, add healthy/ambiguous controls, hidden golds, cleanup, and independent reference/known-bad graders.
5. Use CK-X only as a static architecture reference. Define an original assessment schema with separate candidate prompt, private setup, private semantic/hard-state checks, and no answer file in the candidate-visible artifact. Do not copy CK-X questions or validators.
6. Run a contamination suite containing exact, normalized, structural, and semantic matches against the qualified public exercise sources. Prove that an exact CKAD exercise, a lightly renamed manifest, and a validator-derived shortcut are rejected from the private split.
7. Add a source-policy classifier test with an official curriculum, CC BY documentation, MIT exercise, GPL exercise, no-license repository, BSL simulator, authorized access-controlled simulator, and prohibited dump description. Require the intended use and rights decision before any content enters storage.
8. Have a Kubernetes subject-matter expert and rights reviewer inspect the first converted case. Promote it only when current-version reference and known-bad controls pass, source wording/answers are absent, lineage is complete, and its task adds operational behavior beyond an exam objective.

The pilot succeeds when curriculum coverage is reproducible without becoming benchmark composition; licensed retrieval is distinct from hidden gold; source policy blocks prohibited and unauthorized content; public-answer contamination is detected; an independently authored case passes environment and grader controls; and every resulting artifact has attributable lineage and an allowed use. It does not succeed because an agent scores well on public practice questions or because a public repository contains many files named `q1` through `q20`.
